#3990. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#3988. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

If you're excited to jump in tomorrow, be sure to check out these Free Monopoly Go Dice Links before you dive into the new content.

#3987. 'That's An Error' - Xbox Engineer Denies 360 Games Are Being Teased For Disc To Digital

Update [Fri 13th Nov 2026, 5:45pm]: Well, unfortunately we have answer - Xbox engineer Eden Marie has confirmed over on BlueSky that the inclusion of Fable III in this image was an "error".

While the post itself is private, it reads as follows (and thanks to Pure Xbox user TheBillConiglio for alerting us to this):

"Bill: Seeing an image of a library with Fable 3 having a disc to digital badge. Error, or......"

Original Story: Yesterday, Xbox starting rolling out three new console features for Xbox Insiders to try out: rotating home backgrounds, the ability to choose which side the Xbox guide pops open on, and new ways to organise disc to digital games.

They're all cool features that we're definitely keen to play around with, but what got our attention most was the image Xbox used to show off the new disc to digital update. Particularly, the games featured with the D2D licence icon plopped in the bottom-left corner of each game tile.

Did Xbox just tease the inclusion of Xbox 360 games in the D2D programme? Well, that would be true if the image depicting Fable III is to be taken at face value. At a glance, you'd probably see the image above and think, 'great, that's awesome', but the more you look at it, the weirder it gets.

Avowed famously launched on Xbox without a physical disc. So, if the theory about Xbox 360 games joining the programme is on the money, does that mean we're getting a physical copy of Avowed too? And what about Age of Empires IV? That never received a physical release either. Then If we really want to go Enola Holmes on this image, Forza games aren't D2D compatible.

We're thinking someone at Xbox might've messed up with this image. Announcements of this magnitude shouldn't be buried in an Xbox Insider update. Xbox should be shouting about it on the front page. So, why do an Xbox 360 game and two digital-only titles have D2D icons attached to them? I could think of a lazy reason.

Only time will tell, but consider us sceptical for now. We've chalked this one up to a blunder from Xbox, although it wouldn't surprise us if Xbox 360 games did eventually join the D2D programme. And hey, it's Xbox's birthday this Sunday. Maybe there's more to this than meets the eye.

@BacklogBrad the issue isn't with converting 360 or OG XBox game discs to digital versions, the issue is that those discs don't have a unique identifier assigned to them (this started with the XBox One generation, and not all of the early XBox One games have them).

Without the UID there's no way to assign a specific disc to the digital license, meaning one disc could be used to grant anyone digital access to that game. The UID prevents this as you need to revalidate the disc licence periodically, and if you sell the disc / lend it to someone, it will validate on their device, which will invalidate your license the next time your console does an online check in.

#3985. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#3984. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.

#3983. Talking Point: What Are You Playing This Weekend? (14th November)

Well folks, you've made it through another week – well done! Chances are many of you have completed your quest in Ocarina of Time by now, with many more of you eagerly awaiting your next jaunt across Leonida when GTA 6 launches on the 19th.

Going back to OoT for a moment, Nintendo confirmed this week that it managed to sell over 5 million copies in just 4 days – astonishing! The company also revealed some behind-the-scenes info about the ReDead enemies, while we took at look at what we think are some of the best 'tiny tweaks' in the remake.

Elsewhere, Nintendo announced it will be ceasing Apple and Google sign-ins on Nintendo Accounts, while the Switch 2 received yet another system update.

Reviews this week include Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy (7/10), Queen's Domain (9/10), Metaphor ReFantazio (8/10), and Harold Halibut (7/10).

Talking Point With Big Walk, The AI-In-Game-Dev Debate Just Got A Lot Murkier

Talking Point What's Your Favourite Tiny Tweak In Zelda: Ocarina Of Time?

I had plans to possibly play the Xbox or PS5 Pro this weekend (they’ve been neglected) but it seems like I have bigger fish to fry on my Switch 2! I played majority of Harold Halibut this week for the review and I’m so close to the end. It’s only right I should finish it yeah?

Once that’s ticked off the backlog, I have more progress to make in Final Fantasy Resonance and I might even dare to play OoT more if I have the time. No doubt something will spoil my plans so my backup might be a Peak session with my pals.

Not the best of weekends for city integrity because both Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered and Earth Defense Force 5 continue to delight my free time. I am still hooked on Tape to Tape with a few teams left to unlock. I made the mistake of buying Warhammer Survivors and I fear the combination of 40k/Age of Sigmar lore with the Vampire Survivors addictive game loop will be the downfall of my productivity elsewhere. On the 16-bit retro-front I got Legend of Galactic Heroes on the Super Famicom. This has been on my bucket list for decades, and I'm glad to report the game lives up to the brilliant source material.

Game of the week is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Everyone has probably completed the game by now, but I am still on the way to Zora’s Domain. I was there, Gandalf, 28 years ago when the original released on N64, thus I know what to do and where to go to, quickly breezing through the game like the Star Fox reboot. I am slowly enjoying the journey, a bit jealous for all the players experiencing this journey for the first time. Dare I dream for F-Zero X to get similar love next year?

Queen's Domain has got me royally hooked. After a somewhat confusing and frustrating start, I'm now deep into the game in all but actual progression, and its classic PC stylings and game design are just ticking so many boxes I'd forgotten I had.

It's still frustrating, but lord help me am I going to push on through this weekend.

So I played Alone in the Dark last weekend, as promised. It's not great. However, Queen's Domain is great, so I definitely plan to put a bit more time into it over the next few days or so.

Despite the very minor upgrades, I'm also keen to dive into Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy. The visuals have definitely received a nice bump in quality, so it'll be nice to experience the campaign in glorious 4K.

I have other games that I want to squeeze in before 2026 is up, but I simply haven't been able to pry myself away from Ocarina of Time yet. I was so unsure about it from the initial reveal, but goodness me, I love this remake so much.

Despite my best efforts to stretch it out for as long as possible, I only have a few dungeons to go at this point. I'm going to be a wreck at the finale.

The kids and I are heading up Death Mountain this weekend, although by the time you read this we’ve probably already done in Dodongo and are beansing it to Zora’s Domain.

Unfortunately, playing through Ocarina my spawn means that I can’t continue once they’ve gone to bed. And yet despite having dozens of 2026's finest to be getting on with (finished Mixtape this week, great stuff), I’m stuck in a very enjoyable COD funk, with all sorts of numbers in multiplayer. Have a good one, folks.

Those are our plans, but what about yours? Let us know what you'll be slapping in your Switch (2) in the poll below.

Nintendo Life’s resident horror fanatic, when he’s not knee-deep in Resident Evil and Silent Hill lore, Ollie likes to dive into a good horror book while nursing a lovely cup of tea. He also enjoys long walks and listens to everything from TOOL to Chuck Berry.

Well, after last week’s rather unfortunate timing of my daughter falling ill on the very day Ocarina of Time launched, I’m delighted to report she’s made a full recovery and has officially started nursery! A big week of milestones in our household, both in Hyrule and the real world.

As for Link, things have escalated rather dramatically. I met a lovely sage who kindly aged me seven years, returned to Castle Town to find the neighbourhood had gone downhill somewhat, and encountered a deeply unsettling graveyard child with a worrying obsession with skull masks.

Since then, I’ve managed to keep pace with the restless soul of Dampé, who rewarded my efforts with a shiny new Hookshot, and I’m now knee deep in the Forest Temple. I’ve also accidentally consumed an alarming number of poes. Don’t ask.

I’m hoping to keep up a steady pace of a temple or two a week from here, all while enjoying the build-up to a very special Christmas as my beautiful daughter approaches her first birthday. Watching her discover the world while I rediscover Hyrule feels rather fitting, really.

Tonight I'm not seeing my friends so I'll just continue with my schedule:

Ultros: starting my 3rd time-loop, really curious how this will go and hoping I'm not heading to a dead-end XD

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort: been playing Island Crown at Tennis and Bowling, and unlocking all sorts of queer items 🤭. Ah, that good old Wii Sports! 😍

Tetris Effect: Connected: participating in the weekend ritual, as usual ...

And SMB Wonder, RP Groove and MK World will be the three multiplayer contenders...

Have fun, happy gaming, and make the most of your weekend! ✌🏻🧡🎮

Sonic Generations: The 3DS version, specifically. It's absolutely terrible. I've played a lot of bad Sonic games, but this is something else. I'm currently at the final boss and I feel like I've sunk into the centre of the Triceratops poop in Jurassic Park. The controls just don't make sense; sometimes they behave exactly as they should, while sometimes they literally do the exact opposite of what I've pressed. I don't know if I'll finish this game, but I do know that if I don't finish it then I won't lose sleep over it.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026): I rolled credits on this last night and… wow. No game is truly perfect but, as a remake, this is perfect. Faithful yet tweaked where you'd want it to be, and utterly gorgeous on top. It feels weird to say that a 2026 remake of a 1998 game is my game of the year so far and worth buying a Switch 2 for, but Ocarina of Time is my game of the year so far and worth buying a Switch 2 for.

Professor Layton and the Curious Village: I'm still chipping away at this; a few puzzles here, a few puzzles there. Will I ever finish it? Who knows? Does it still make me feel like a dullard incredibly frequently? Yes.

Super Mario 3D Land and New Super Mario Bros. 2: There are still secret exits and star coins to find, and I will find them all!

Additionally, even though I've played through Ocarina of Time, Skyward Sword HD and Tears of the Kingdom over the past few months, I'm already hankering for more Zelda. I'm torn between A Link Between Worlds, or either of Oracle of Ages/Oracle of Seasons. I've not played any of them before. Or maybe I do yet another playthrough of The Minish Cap? 👀

I’ve also accidentally consumed an alarming number of poes. Don’t ask.

This weekend I will be working towards the endgame of Final Fantasy Resonance. Just reached the big reveal of Umbra's identity which I guessed ages ago but despite some predictability in the narrative I still think the writing is really strong and I'm connecting with the characters in a way I have with the best Final Fantasy games prior.

Will also put more time into the excellent Queen's Domain. The game is really starting to open up now that I have evolved a weapon and bested the first boss netting the big game changer traversal reward for that accomplishment. Still have to play with the utmost caution but I love the game so far.

Finally more Street Fighter 6 and Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered with the kids. At the request of my son we'll also put more time into Super Smash Bros. Ultimate. I hadn't played in years so he stomped me the first few rounds but my muscle memory kicked in and I sent him packing to Kingdom Hearts with Sora.

More OOT of course 👍 Still only in the early game as Ive had a lot on, in and out of work. Equally, I dont want to rush the experience as every moment I am thoroughly enjoying.

Im in the market for another CRT so might do some hunting for one to add to my retro setup.

Rest of the weekend, probably some Burnout Takedown. 170+ events in the game and Im trying to get gold in each.

Well, this was quite a week in terms of reducing and expanding the backlogs. I'm finally through with Nonograms Prophecy...at least with what I could access of it because the last two Big Picture slots still say "in progress" while solving everything else in the mode still left the counter at 0/10 (a remarkable counter in itself because there are 9 big pictures without the unplayable tutorial as is, 11 with the missing stuff and 12 if you do count the tutorial). Might be DLC stuff but the page shows no signs of the latter, and honestly? After 40 hours, I think I'm good.😄

I've also finally wrapped up Wolfenstein: The New Order and dipped my toes into The Old Blood, but The New Colossus is more of a priority now. Where to install it, though? Ah, that's a whole other story. The 512 Gb Express SanDisk gambled with at a regional online marketplace (after the only Minsk retailer previously stocking it messaged me back about not getting any more stuff shipped in) arrived last Sunday night, getting properly recognized by the console right on pickup... then repeatedly heating up and autoejected in the laptop beyond 4 Gb of data (from the backups to avoid redownloading). I had done enough reading about online marketplace fakes and their proverbial real capacity that my immediate reactions defy sharing here in public, but tested the thing in Switch 2 again... and it does work there?🤔 Everything from the previously installed stuff to the newly added FFXIV trial and the retrieved Gamecube app downloaded and proceeded to run without a hitch. Knocking on wood here, but the bullet may have been ultimately dodged.

Anyhoo, the Gen 10 storage expansion with roughly 80 Gb left of it even urged me to pull the trigger on the juicy FFVIIR discounts after all, although both games are 10 Gb bigger, unlikely to get completed before Xenoblade 3's bloa- er, upgraded filesize arrives (not to mention next year's Genesis) and still probably best benched at least until I finish Crisis Core. What did get installed from the spoils of the same eShop top-up is Drop Duchy and Souldiers, if at the expense of Vampire Hunters on OLED. What? New Colossus? Right - so the aforementioned 256 Gb card became predictably vacant and I'm still too unenthused about last gen's period of juggling multiple cards per console (what with repeatedly powering on and off in the process) to use it properly, so I really just went and boosted Mariko's storage towards many a previously shelved playthrough instead. New Colossus and Biomutant, Haven and Snake Pass, Layers of Fear 2 and Mad Rat Dead, Immortals and Starlink, Amalur and Dragon's Dogma, Outer Worlds and Pillars of Eternity, Astral Chain and Nocturne, Nelke and WoFF, Diablo 2 and Rebel Galaxy Outlaw, Red Dead Redemption and Devil Ma- never mind, the last one promptly got kicked back out to accommodate New Colossus last night. No, no room left to immediately reinstall Vampire Hunters but you can't win them all.

Needless to say, the weekend's hybrid appetites are encompassing the whole list above alongside the OLED's (Ball x Pit, Drop Duchy, KH1, Eternia, Yumia, Potion Permit, DerQ, and AC2) and NS2's (Motorfest, RE4, FFXIV, Cyberpunk, Tales of Arise, XC2 and Factorio) respective troves. Barely even making plans for the handhelds as a result, although some Flotsam, Xenosaga, Gravity Rush and Chase Begins may still show up on the menu. And that's enough of my first world pseudoblog.😅

#3982. "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"

Unionised workers reiterate call for a "solid offer" for Arkane Lyon's future

Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Published by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - one of two unions who represent workers at Arkane, the other being Printemps écologique, who didn't issue a similar message - the official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine". It maintains that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. The writers then take Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuse the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 11th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.

#3981. 'We Want to Create Franchises That Withstand Decades': Sony Reveals Ambition to Dominate Anime

Sony’s gradual transition from consumer electronics to entertainment giant is paying dividends, as the firm’s value continues to rise on the back of hits like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the overall PlayStation business.

But the manufacturer has one big ambition that will bring all its divisions together: anime.

A big Bloomberg report, focusing on subsidiary Aniplex’s boss Atsuhiro Iwakami, shed some light on the firm’s strategy. It’s moving aggressively to dominate an industry that’s booming in popularity worldwide.

Iwakami points to Demon’s Slayer as justification for its approach.

Its first movie, 2020’s Mugen Soul, dethroned Spirited Away to become Japan’s highest-grossing film. Its successor, 2025’s Infinity Castle, went on to gross almost $1 billion worldwide.

Iwakami’s goal is simple: to find or create the next One Piece, a franchise that could become the centrepiece of its entertainment division for potentially decades to come.

As the article points out, anime unifies all of Sony’s divisions in an unprecedented way: content can be created by Aniplex, distributed by Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures, promoted by PlayStation (where there’s an inherent overlap in audiences), and even supported by Sony Music (anime theme songs et al are wildly popular).

To support its ambitions, the company has become one of the biggest investors in light novel powerhouse Kadokawa, and Iwakami admits it would invest in sector stalwart Shueisha as well should the opportunity arise.

But original content will be foundational to Sony moving forwards, as it faces aggressive competition from Netflix and Disney, both of which are competing for content in the wake of the anime boom.

Sony ultimately wants a franchise it owns outright, where it can control all merchandise sales and more.

It recently founded a new studio, Hayate, as part of a joint collaboration between Aniplex and Crunchyroll. Its remit is to create original anime for a global audience.

Next year, Sony will add an anime tab to the PS5’s homepage, giving it another opportunity to promote its content to players around the world.

I’m particularly interested to see if PS Studios is eventually recruited to create original games based on some of these properties, and how it approaches those.

Obviously, if the goal is to create franchises that reach as many people worldwide as possible, then exclusivity may not necessarily be the play here.

But while Sony already has a strong foot in the door, it admits it’s still at the start of its strategy right now. It’s going to be interesting to see how things evolve over the coming years.

Talking Point Sony's Investing in Anime, But Why Isn't PlayStation Leading the Charge?

News PS5 to Integrate Anime into Main Menu as Sony Tightens Ties with Crunchyroll

"Anime and gaming have overlapping communities"

As the Editor of Push Square, Sammy has over 15 years of experience analysing the world of PlayStation, from PS3 through PS5 and everything in between. #3980. Former Xbox First-Party Game 'Kiln' Gets A New Identity And Its Biggest Update Of All Time

When Double Fine released Kiln as an Xbox first-party title last year, it's fair to say a lot of the Xbox fanbase was baffled by it. As much as it was a good game (we gave it a 7/10 in our Pure Xbox review), it also shipped with just a singular, online-only mode that was bound to get old pretty quickly.

Double Fine ended up being let go by Xbox, turning Kiln from an Xbox first-party game into an independent game, and it received a brand-new update back in September, adding a new creative game mode along with various other features.

But today, to mark the planned end of development, it's received its biggest update of all time - adding in three new game modes, an increased level cap, a Photo Booth and loads more besides.

Here's a look at just the highlights of this new update:

In terms of the three modes, Fire Fighter is a 4v4 mode where "both teams are in a mad dash to catch a flaming Chimenea", Stoked is also a 4v4 mode that's "all about igniting the Pyres with your team’s flame", and Local Mini Quench is a smaller version of the original Quench mode that can be played with up to three other people offline.

Offline mode is actually classed as a separate new feature as well:

"As part of being able to play locally, we’ve added an offline mode. This allows you to play and practice without needing to worry about your Ping or people. This, alongside the player hosted matches and account change, helps future-proof Kiln so that you can play it for years to come!"

Pretty cool, right? On top of that, Kiln has received a brand-new identity this week in the form of "Kiln: Reshaped", with the name change serving as a way to "let you know how much is in this update!".

Unfortunately, it does seem like Kiln's flame has already been doused for the majority of players at this point, but it's great to see Double Fine putting in the work to not only preserve it for the future, but hopefully light the spark once again for people who have fallen away from it in recent months.

Don't forget it's on Xbox Game Pass as well, or available on the Xbox Store for just £6.99 / $7.99.

Mega Crit expects "to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready" for the main game

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Slay the Spire 2's early access journey continues, and developer Mega Crit isn't skimping on what it's calling the roguelike deckbuilder's "biggest update yet." Update v0.113.0 goes into beta today, introducing a new character in The Fool. It also adds two new game modes, called Blitz and Dread.

"Wah!! The first new character for Early Access arrives," Mega Crit enthuses in the patch notes. "A silly musician who wields a bow! How can such a whimsical creature survive within the Spire? Why, that's up to you! We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch. Even more importantly, be sure to have fun figuring out all the strategies and story of this gently bard. It would be foolish not to!"

If you want to opt into the beta branch and check out The Fool before the character is ready for the main game, just hop into the game's properties on Steam, go into the Game Versions & Betas tab, and select "public-beta" from the dropdown menu.

On top of the new character, there are two new game modes Blitz is "condensed and chaotic deckbuilding-focused mode" where the "Merchant's wares feel a bit off, the map is gone, and Gold no longer matters." Dread is a "brutally difficult mode" that requires you to reach Ascension on every character – including the Fool – to even take a run at.

A few months ago, Mega Crit said it was slowing down on updates so it could focus on "bigger, more impactful content," and it looks like we're starting to see the fruits of that pivot. Slay the Spire 2 launched back in March, and expect the game's early access period to be similar to the year-and-a-half it took the previous game to reach version 1.0, so it looks like we've got a fair few more updates to look forward to in the meantime.

#3978. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.

#3976. You can now play Pillars of Eternity and Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire with a controller on PC from start to finish, thanks to a new update open for testing

Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also gotten a makeover

After gifting Pillars of Eternity a turn-based mode for its tenth anniversary, Obsidian have now rolled out full PC controller support for both the RPG and its younger sibling Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire. The support, along with some tweaks to Deadfire's turn-based mode, are currently out in public test form.

"You can now play the whole of either game with a controller, from character creation to the end credits (and, in Deadfire, all the way out to naval combat), in both real-time with pause and turn-based mode," the studio wrote in their announcement of the public test going live. "Deadfire’s support builds on the controller scheme from the console editions. Prefer to switch things up? Pick up your mouse and keyboard at any time, and the game follows right along."

"Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also been reworked with the improvements we made for Pillars of Eternity’s turn-based mode: turns now follow each character’s speed, combat is more lethal, and swapping weapons or drinking potions no longer costs your action. You can now switch turn-based mode on or off during a playthrough, and the update brings a long list of fixes across combat, quests, audio, and the interface."

Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are included in the support, along with the Steam Deck and Steam's Big Picture mode. Radial menus have been worked in to allow rapid firing of abilities, spells, and party commands, with the interface also popping up the right button prompts for your controller of choice.

These additions are all part of Patch 1.3.10.0, the full notes for which can be found in the post I've embedded above, alongside instructions on how to get into the public test. The patch also does things like ensure "the description of Fulvano’s Boots is no longer fragmented". I'm glad Obsidian have saved those soles.

The studio haven't put a concrete end date on the test at this point, instead noting it "will run for some time as we continue to update it in preparation for a full release". As it's a test, those jumping in should expect bugs and other funkiness.

#3975. Forza Horizon 6 Content Roadmap Revealed For Late 2026 & 2027

With a specific focus on January and February of next year

Ready for some more news on Forza Horizon 6? The team at Playground Games has announced a content roadmap for the game today, pulling the curtain back on their plans for the end of 2026 and all of next year.

You can get loads of detail about all of this in the video up above, but in a nutshell, we're getting Series 8 "Horizon Holidays" and Series 9 "Legendary Explorers" before the year is out. Then, as we head into January and February, Series 10 will be based around "Exotics and Tuners", while other new additions include a permanent new radio station, absolutely loads of new Reward Cars, and various other bits and bobs.

Most importantly, the first expansion for the game will also be released in January of 2027. Playground Games still doesn't want to talk about it just yet, but apparently we'll be hearing about it very soon.

News Forza Horizon 6's First Premium Expansion Planned For January 2027 Alongside PS5 Launch

Sony fans loved FH5, will they vibe with FH6? Probably

As you can see from the rest of this roadmap, the remainder of 2027 gets more vague for now, but it's confirmed that a second expansion is on the way along with a Festival Playlist overhaul, new race routes and various other new features.

They do talk quite a lot about the Festival Playlist overhaul in the video up above, so again, it's well worth a watch if you want to know more about what's on the way to Forza Horizon 6 in the future.

All of this sounds pretty good to us, and considering how the game has come in for a little bit of disgruntlement in recent months, it's clear to see that Playground Games is hoping for a strong 2027 when it comes to new FH6 content.

#3974. Opinion: Nintendo Made Ocarina Of Time's Best Moment Even Better

Before launch, I didn't think it would be possible for anyone to spoil Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 for me.

I've played through the N64 original more times than I care to admit, and know it better than just about any other game out there. That said, if someone had told me about the Master Sword moment in the remake before I got to it, I would have been really upset.

And so, let's consider this a formal warning. If you haven't made it to the moment when Link first pulls the Master Sword from its Temple of Time pedestal in the Switch 2 remake yet, then stop reading right now and only return once you have seen it for yourself. It is spectacular, but it's something that warrants going in completely blind to really hit home. You have been warned.

You know what, I'm even going to stick a picture of Darunia below, just so that the coming paragraphs aren't spoiledFair does by an over-zealous scroll. This is your last chance to turn back!

Okay, all clear? Let's talk about how incredible the new Master Sword cutscene is.

This moment in the original is one of my foundational gaming memories. The score, the blue lighting, the threat of Ganondorf's giant looming face. It's all just chef's kiss levels of fantastic.

Knowing full well that my partner didn't know the mid-game twist — and desperate to show her the first walk out of the Temple of Time and the source of so much childhood trauma — I called her in and promised her a slice of "peak gaming". I thought we had seen almost all of its new form in the remake trailers.

But I was very wrong. Even in a game as well-known a quantity as this, Nintendo still had a surprise up its sleeve.

And so, we sat together as Link first pulled the Master Sword from the pedestal. I had a little cry as he swung the sword around, and I was ready to move straight to the Chamber of Sages lore dump. What I didn't expect was a full-blown cinematic from the gates of the Sacred Realm, some bonus Ganondorf content, and an image so threatening that it definitely would have given me nightmares for weeks had it been in the original.

I'm talking about rocky Link, petrified with the Master Sword in hand as Ganondorf taunts him while sauntering his way to the Triforce.

It follows the already stunning image of Link opening the door to the Sacred Realm itself, awash with dreamy lighting and colouring, making the pivot to dread all the more impactful. I'm a particular fan of the Ganondorf motif sting right as Link turns to stone. It's all so chilling!

I was seeing one of my most-replayed games from a new perspective.

What a fantastic surprise, as well. I've loved all of the little extra cutscenes in the remake and the bonus context they provide (a particular shoutout to the Kokiri watching the Great Deku Tree's leaves fall), but this one felt like the first moment that I was seeing one of my most-replayed games from a new perspective. My imagination had filled in Ganondorf's menace and Link's helplessness in the N64 original, but never quite like this.

It was made all the more special to be watching it with someone who had no idea what was coming next. While I gasped and cried at seeing images that I had only ever imagined, she did the same, witnessing all the drama for the first time. Honestly, there's nothing quite like seeing someone's jaw drop at their first realisation of the time jump.

Such a special moment is carried into its follow-up scene. After returning to the Temple of Time and meeting Sheik, you walk into Hyrule as you now find it, destroyed and crumbling at the hands of Ganondorf.

While there's something innately unsettling about the N64's handling of this moment (the silence of the Temple courtyard contrasted with the first scream of a ReDead is wonderful), the remaster dedicates another short cutscene to highlighting everything that's gone wrong.

Panning over the decimated rooftops to Ganon's Castle in the distance, it really showcases just how broken the world has become in Link's seven years away. There's an argument to be made that everything is more sinister if you're forced to imagine it (look at how scary Jaws is before you see the shark), but man, what a feeling it is to finally see it realised after decades of keeping it in my head.

The remake isn't something that I want to rush, so I'm making sure that I go slow. I still have some of my favourite temples, bosses and puzzles to come, but if this is how it handles my favourite moment in the game (maybe in all of gaming), then I'm going to need to buy another box of tissues.

What do you make of the new Master Sword moment in Ocarina of Time? Let us know in the comments.

As a kid I never owned OoT on the 64 - for some reason I just had Majora's Mask so that one holds all the early 3D Zelda nostalgia points for me. I didn't get into OoT until the GameCube version. The original is clearly a masterpiece, but it always felt like... a playable stage play? Or reading a book where you already know all the key plot points through cultural osmosis? It never felt like a special, personal experience for me.

The remake completely changes that. Now it's deeply personal, extremely moving. It's amazing what a new art direction, set dressings, musical score, some extra dialog, and a few more small cutscenes in key moments can do.

It's still the same underlying game, but it hits so much harder. The way you can see the Deku Tree looming over the forest village in the beginning, and then the cutscene after you finish the first child dungeon... You really feel the effect that moment has on the Kokiri.

Or even the redesigned entrance to the ice cavern. Where before it was some generic looking cave you stumble upon, now it really looks and feels like the source of the freeze - from the snowy wind to the imposing entrance to the cavern, like everything in the area is visually drawing you toward that entrance now.

So many little things that are executed perfectly and add up to make this game an emotional experience like it never was before. Characters feel like real people with lives and desires rather than pawns in a larger plot. All it takes is a few more facial animations, lines of dialog reacting to events, and better camera angles and lighting during pivotal moments.

Oh and last thing, holy crap does each dungeon feel like a unique place, a real location that means something to the surrounding area - each one having its own music (as it did in the original) and enhanced so much visually in this remake to really set them apart, it provides such a stark contrast to the more generic shrines and such from BotW/TotK. It shows how great the classic Zelda formula can really be with modern technology and care put into each location.

They really mastered the nostalgia and classic moments while making it feel new for longtime players who have torn Hyrule apart for all it's secrets and hundreds of hours of gameplay

25 OG Xbox titles are now on PC, and it's an utterly bizarre list of games

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This weekend marks Xbox's 25th birthday, and while any celebration of the milestone is going to be muted in view of the layoff bloodbath Microsoft is currently engaging in, the gaming division is taking steps to keep us thinking about the brand in a positive light. That includes a fresh expansion to the list of original Xbox games that are now backwards compatible on PC.

After the four original Xbox games that Microsoft brought to PC earlier this year, another 21 have joined the list – a total of 25 games for the console's 25th birthday. The new list of games is an utterly bizarre one, largely dominated by LucasArts titles. That includes plenty of beloved Star Wars titles, alongside largely forgotten obscurities like Secret Weapons Over Normandy and Thrillville.

Some of the titles you might recognize, like Star Wars classics Battlefront 2, Jedi Outcast, and Knights of the Old Republic, are odd choices in themselves, since those games are already available on PC. Assuming Xbox is using the same emulation-based solution to port these games, they're all going to be substantially worse experiences than simply picking up the native PC versions for the same price on Steam.

That goes double for The Elder Scrolls 3: Morrowind, which is also on the list of newly added games. The Xbox version of Morrowind was a stunning technical achievement back in 2002, but it was notoriously janky even at the time, filled with bugs and technical limitations that have been robustly addressed on PC. I struggle to come up with a compelling reason anyone would want to play this version over the PC original today, especially with all the mods available for the RPG.

There are two games I absolutely will not complain about, however: TimeSplitters 2 and TimeSplitters: Future Perfect. Developed by the Rare veterans at Free Radical Design, the TimeSplitters series was a spiritual successor to classic N64 games GoldenEye and Perfect Dark, refreshing the FPS gameplay for a new generation with fun weapon gimmicks and charmingly goofy characters.

TimeSplitters never moved beyond cult classic status, and attempts to revive the series ended in failure. None of these games ever got PC ports, which makes their inclusion arguably the most notable part of this Xbox backwards compatibility update.

His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest big action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator.

#3972. Goddess of Victory: Nikke's PC launcher suffers potential malware infection, with its publishers suggesting folks who've booted since late September do a security check

A cruel twist for the Shift Up-developed epic shooter RPG of cruel humanity destiny

Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a gacha shooter/RPG developed by Stellar Blade makers Shift Up, has suffered a "security incident" which has seen its PC launcher potentially be infected with third-party malware. Thankfully, it seems a patch to make the launcher safe again has been quickly dished out, but publishers Level Infinite are still advising players who've booted the game up since September 27th to do some security checks.

"We have identified that some files in the NIKKE Windows PC launcher were recently tampered with by a third party, potentially allowing malicious programs to run when the launcher was launched," the developers of the game with anime girls who - judging by the promo art - breast boobily announced yesterday. "As a result, your PCs and account information may have been exposed to security risks.

"We are continuing to investigate the extent of the potential damage and review appropriate response measures. We are also conducting a thorough review of our network security environment, including our CDN, to determine how the PC launcher files were compromised. We will take all necessary precautions to prevent further damage and ensure that this issue does not happen again. We deeply regret that this security incident has caused Commanders significant concern and distress, when our responsibility should have been to provide a safe gaming environment."

In order to try and help players "scan for and remove the malicious programs distributed in this incident", publishers Level Infinite have added a feature to Nikke's official PC client that does just that. They're advising that anyone who's booted up the game at least once after September 27th at 15:41 (UTC+9) use that or perform a manual security check.

Once that's done, affected players are advised to change the passwords for any accounts they've used on the PC they used to boot the launcher, as well as generate new API keys and access tokens. "We take very seriously the possibility that this incident may have affected not only your gaming experience but also your PC, accounts with external services, and personal assets," Level Infinite added. "If you believe you may have been affected by this issue or suffered from any loss, please contact our customer support team. We will review each inquiry carefully and respond as promptly as possible."

Going forwards, they plan to improve their monitoring "so that any unauthorized file modifications or security threats can be detected early and addressed promptly", as well as "establish an integrity verification system for external resources accessed by the PC launcher" and ensure the launcher only requires "the minimum permissions necessary".

Here's hoping the studio are able to keep things more secure in the future and that affected players are able to get rid of any malware with minimal suffering or inconvenience.

#3971. Mini Review: Shrek 2 Remastered (PS5) - Far Far Away Gets an All-Star Makeover

I believe, I believe, I believe this is a good time

Version Reviewed: PS5 (Standard) / European

While DreamWorks' tales of an ogre and his mates are hit or miss, there's no denying that Shrek 2 Remastered is a winning overhaul of a mid-2000s gem.

It comes from an era when movie tie-in games were all the rage, whether that meant half-arsed Harry Potter adventures or excellent efforts like X-Men Origins: Wolverine.

Shrek 2 is a thoroughly joyous time, adopting a Marvel Ultimate Alliance-style formula for its antics. Shrek, Fiona, and Donkey form the core team you'll swap between, with familiar faces like Lil Red and the Gingerbread Man joining the squad from time to time.

Each character packs special abilities, whether that's Donkey's 'Burro Blast' or Fiona's power to slow down time, Matrix-style. It's incredibly silly, and never commented on by our delightful cast. We wouldn't have it any other way.

Across a variety of locales from the titular movie, you'll squash, splatter, and swashbuckle through puzzles that take advantage of everyone's unique abilities.

Whether that's using Shrek's strength to hurl chickens into a pen for a fast food chain, or Donkey's agility to sneak up on a goblin that poops gems in a museum, there's plenty of variety.

'Hero Time' moments also spice things up, ranging from QTEs involving Fiona singing (badly) to birds, to Donkey riding Elizabeth the Dragon in a fiery chase.

There's more depth here than your usual movie game slop, too, with friendly leprechaun Crazy Larry selling stat increases and upgrades in exchange for your hard-earned coins. It scratches that familiar LEGO game itch of smashing objects, platforming, and exploring every nook and cranny for collectibles.

All of it looks and sounds the part, with a faithful recreation of DreamWorks' fantastical art direction and an appropriately over-the-top score.

Where Shrek 2 Remastered really comes together is its brand-new co-op multiplayer. Played locally or online, the latter requiring an Epic Games Account, you can team up with three other players. It's a neat inclusion for a game that's over two decades old.

There's also a basic but enjoyable Photo Mode, perfect for capturing some amusing shots of the gang.

Performance on base PS5 is generally stable, although frame drops occasionally rear their ugly heads during crowded skirmishes or when loading new areas. Paired with an occasionally awkward camera, these blemishes don't hurt the experience too much.

Shrek 2 Remastered doesn't quite polish away all the rough edges of its original release, but there's so much charm here that it's difficult to hold them against it.

With a varied adventure, plenty of laughs, and the welcome addition of online co-op, this is a lovely reminder of when movie tie-in games could be just as entertaining as the films that inspired them.

#3970. Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim

Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

Playground Games is ramping up its marketing efforts for its upcoming Fable revival, and a new gameplay showcase seems to confirm the return of enemy Nymphs, which we haven't seen since the original Fable back in 2004.

The new Official Quest Gameplay trailer, released as part of Xbox's 25th anniversary shenanigans, shows a darker side to Albion than we're used to seeing, and I mean that literally. After cranking up the brightness on my monitor, I could see that the footage shows a female hero character seeking out her village's mysterious assailant with the help of a character named Arden. Tracing the attacker's path leads the duo through a heavily wooded forest with giant thorny vines and eventually, a confrontation with some familiar-looking foes outside a cave entrance.

Again, everything is dark in this trailer, but from what I can tell these fellas look a whole lot like the Wood Nymphs, which are one of two species of fairy-like creatures, the other being Water Nymphs, from OG Fable back in the day. They're referred to as "cursed monsters" in the quest log, but c'mon, those are fairies. They're little magical winged humanoids with big heads and tree bark-like skin, and they flutter around in clouds of colorful orbs and shoot ethereal projectiles your way. If that isn't a Wood Nymph, well then I don't know what a Wood Nymph is. And believe me, I know a thing or two about Wood Nymphs.

Anyway, otherwise the trailer is fairly unremarkable. Not in a bad way, just in a way that doesn't reveal anything super new or exciting to talk about, which makes sense considering we're just a few short months away from getting to play the game. Fable is out on PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC on February 23.

#3968. Apex Legends adds a grumpy, teamwiping Godzilla to its growing history of unappealing crossovers

No doubt eager as peas to help pay off EA's billions in debt, battle royale shooter Apex Legends is set to run another of its intellectual propertytastic crossover events. This one, starting on November 10th, stars Godzilla, of Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla vs. Kong, Godzilla (1954), Godzilla 2000: Millennium, Godzilla (1998), Son of Godzilla, and Godzilla (2014). I might be missing some.

Besides a profitable range of weapon and character skins, most of which appear to have hot glue gunned an 70-year film franchise's worth of dorsal fins all over themselves, the King of the Monsters himself will show up on the game's Storm Point map. He does at least have more than a background cameo: he'll occasionally blast an area with Legend-melting atomic breath, though brave souls who risk the danger zone can score a custom Devotion LMG with a unique heat ray attack of its own.

Worth noting also that the character skins are each based on a certain 'zilla movie, though as our freelance news writer and associate Large Lizard Cinema expert Ashley isn't working today, I'm not sure which of these are from hits and which are the duds. Walking wallhack motherfucker Bloodhound gets the newest fashion, their skin being inspired by Minus Zero, while my personal favourite Scottish scientist Horizon gets duds based on Big G in Godzilla vs. Destoroyah. Octane's skin is taken from... something called a Jet Jaguar? Google suggests this may in fact be elite Godzilla knowledge, something I clearly lack.

Regardless, and with the understanding that a lot of effort goes into these crossovers, I still kinda wish they didn't exist? Even putting aside basic game-playing problems with how, for example, wacky skins interfere with Legend silhouettes – you couldn't pay me to initiate a fight against a full team of near-identical Gundampeople - it's just icky to have an otherwise sharp, smart, at times fiercely competitive battle royale turned into an animated billboard for a few days.

Besides, Apex already has its own kaiju: the sleepy, pacifist Leviathans that innocently wandered into the King's Canyon map for a few of the earlier seasons. I consider these much better Friend Material than Godzilla, on the grounds that they'd only kill you by accident, and it was usually your own fault - by wandering under their briefly raised megahooves - anyway.

#3967. Mini Review: Tape To Tape (Switch) - A Great Roguelite For Underserved Hockey Lovers

If you are a hockey fan with a Switch, you have been poorly served by the system’s library. Odd really, considering how well hockey itself translates into video game form. And then you chance upon Tape to Tape drowning in the weekly AI slop eShop releases, a curiously labelled “gorgeous roguelite hockey world" affair. Is this it? Is this the hockey game of my dreams?

Tape to Tape did not sprout magically overnight. It has been a labour of love for several years and has been feeding off a lively player community with feedback to shape the version now in our hands. Forget about offsides, penalties, and other obtuse rules (unless you pick the Modern Squad): this is hardcore old-school hockey the likes of which we haven't seen since NHL Hitz and that is a very good thing indeed.

While this is strictly an offline couch multiplayer affair with all the expected gameplay modes up to four players, the real meat is found in the campaign mode, where its roguelite nature shines. You start with a choice of three teams, with another 16 unlocking as you make progress and meet unlock conditions. Each comes with their own gameplay quirks, with some being significant advantages while others rapidly become heavy handicaps.

In my dozen or so (not all of them successful) runs, there were no two alike, thanks to the sizeable amount of possible combos of team, star players, bench-warmers, unlockable team relics, and individual player skills. A successful run will expose huge chunks of delightfully silly lore and can run to over an hour while you pick your path between opponents' stadiums and a cast of oddball individuals that will (mostly) help to bring out your team's potential.

The other unexpected stars are the opponent teams, from stereotypical spoofs like the soccer team (with easily recognisable caricatures of real-life players) that doesn’t even use sticks to play to the Canadian team that requires tariffs (translating into huge handicaps per period) and has their heads animated in unmistakable South Park fashion, all the way up to the hockey nemesis themselves, the club wielding Golfers in the final campaign act.

And the less said about the cheating Officials team, the better. Having a clean run end abruptly because the official grabs the puck and shoves it into the back of your net might be part of the fun, but it still stings.

Overall, this is a refreshingly addictive take on hockey, with tight gameplay, humour that lands, and rewarding unlockable content. The Switch edition offers something not found on other versions: the option to throw a Joy-Con at other players and have a quick match in tabletop mode. If you grew up with Ice Hockey and Blades of Steel on NES, Mutant League Hockey on Mega Drive, and the all-mighty, all-conquering NHL Hitz on sixth-generation hardware, this game was made for you.

If you have never played a hockey game in your life before and have zero interest in the sport, this game is also for you! Tape to Tape is not just a great hockey video game - it is a great video game, period.
